title: How McBee composes and names tunes
summary: He starts with chords and writes the melody later, recalling Song of Her for Charles Lloyd.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. Enough said. I want to talk — we’re getting time to wrap up here and I so enjoy our conversations. I wanted to ask you about song titles and how they relate to the sound of the music and the intent of the music. We talked a little bit and we mentioned some of Pharoah Sanders’ pieces and Alice Coltrane. Now with your own compositions, do you have titles in mind before you start or does something sort of come to you as the song progresses?

Good question. Excuse me. I might have mentioned before that currently, given this Covid situation, I’ve been working on four compositions. Some tunes, one tune I’ll work on today — to limits, to find limits. Then I might go to another one tomorrow. I’m almost completed. But what I do is, since the very beginning, that is my first composition in New York was a tune called “Song of Her” we mentioned that before. It’s from the second side of the “Forest Flower” album, recorded by Charles Lloyd. There was a moment where I felt sort of sublime, I felt sort of alone, I felt lonely, I felt that I needed some comfort to better express myself in more positive moments of expression etcetera, etcetera. When that feeling occurs I, quite frankly, even at that particular time I would sit at the piano and I would play something that might give me reason to feel more relaxed and more acceptable to a nice sound, and then if that sound pleases me I will try to respond to it with a subsequent sound. And so forth and so forth and so on. And I’ve learned that rather than try to compare that moment with what had prevailed, the uniqueness of it would be that you know write it down at the moment of the situation. And then later on, once you’re complete, now I went through this just yesterday at the piano that’s over there. I’m working on something that’s really, really very nice. It’s like once it’s complete then I will write the melody. In other words the chord changes, the rhythms and everything like that, that comes first, then the melody comes secondary. And that’s like a painting. You add this note, and that note, and that note. Now on paper that corresponds to the feeling of that particular chord and so forth, and then if that’s successful then you might find reason to adventure into another area, maybe four bars at a time. But then the next day you might want to return, and upon returning to some creative moment then you might want to make adjustments to those tones, now that you’re at a new moment, a new eye, you might want to flat that tone or raise that tone or leave that © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

tone alone. And in response to not only what it prevails but it might advance notice crossing the bar line into another situation. So you might want to make changes as you go along you know, instead of using a ninth or a fifth, I might use a sixth that might go down to a two and then, you know, etcetera etcetera. So once the tune is completed then it’s time to name the tune. I’ve got a list of names that come to me occasionally that I’ve written back there in my studio, but none have found worth to these three tunes that are waiting.
